tldr: Even high-accuracy LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) systems suffer from short-horizon jitter in their pose streams. This paper proposes a lightweight module that substantially smooths the output poses using a small fixed-lag continuous-time cubic spline fit, without touching the underlying estimator or its map.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CT-SGAL-LIO. It takes the posterior pose stream from a discrete SGal(3) LIO estimator (LIMOncello), performs covariance-aware robust cubic trajectory fitting over a bounded temporal window, and outputs smoothed poses and velocities at a small fixed lag $t_k^\star = t_k - \ell$.
overview:
Recent LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) methods achieve strong global trajectory accuracy by adopting richer state manifolds, such as the Galilean group $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$, alongside iterated error-state Kalman filtering. However, when downstream tasks like control and planning query poses at high frequencies, an annoying problem emerges: because high-rate IMU propagation alternates with lower-rate LiDAR correction, the pose stream exhibits small oscillations and jumps over short horizons, even when it is globally accurate.

To resolve this local inconsistency, existing methods have typically modified the filter to update on individual points within a scan, or optimized continuous-time trajectories (like splines) directly from raw sensor residuals. But continuous-time optimization from raw data is computationally expensive, prone to failure under aggressive rotations or accelerations, and introduces noticeable delays in state updates.

This led the authors to ask: "Can we smooth the pose stream as a post-processing layer without touching the original LIO estimator or its map?" That is how CT-SGAL-LIO was born. The method maintains recent posterior poses in a short temporal buffer and fits a covariance-weighted cubic polynomial over a local Lie algebra chart. The key insight is to query the pose at a small fixed lag, turning the query into an interpolation point within the observed window. This avoids the volatility of extrapolation while preserving causal (online) operation, recovering a smooth continuous-time trajectory.

Evaluated on 17 sequences across three public benchmarks (GRAND-TOUR, MCD, GEODE) and an extended campus run, CT-SGAL-LIO reduced relative trajectory error (RTE) by up to 70% and cut posterior jumps by 85.4%, all while fully preserving global accuracy (ATE).
contributions: Proposed a causal, fixed-lag continuous-time refinement layer that operates strictly on the output posterior pose stream, without depending on the inner workings, maps, or raw residuals of the underlying LIO estimator.

Formulated a robust cubic polynomial fit on a local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ Lie algebra chart, solved efficiently via covariance-weighted iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) combined with curvature regularization.

Demonstrated on three public datasets (17 sequences) that short-term relative motion error (RTE) can be reduced by up to 70% (9.9–51.1% across all seven GEODE sequences) without degrading global accuracy (ATE).
Showed long-term stability during a 19.5-minute real-world run (around 120,000 states), suppressing inter-pose jumps by 85.4% while shifting the global end-to-start gap by only 4.7 mm.

sections.heading: Why does a robot's trajectory jitter when it is globally accurate?
sections.summary: Even in high-accuracy LiDAR-inertial odometry, the alternation between IMU propagation and LiDAR updates induces micro-oscillations over short horizons. While prior remedies heavily modified the estimator itself, this work proposes a much simpler, highly effective alternative: a fixed-lag continuous-time fitting layer wrapped around the estimator's output.
sections.details:
LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is a core building block for mobile robot localization and mapping. Recently, iterated Kalman filters operating on richer state manifolds—such as the Galilean group $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$ that bundles rotation, translation, velocity, and time—have pushed global estimation accuracy to very high levels.

Yet, whenever downstream controllers or planners request poses at high rates, they run into an unsettling issue: local jitter. This happens because the filter alternates between IMU propagation at hundreds of Hertz and LiDAR correction at tens of Hertz, with estimation errors manifesting differently at each step. Even when the trajectory tracks the map accurately on a global scale, poses bounce and jump when viewed over short time horizons.

Existing countermeasures have largely fallen into two camps. One rewires the filter to update on point-by-point observations (like Point-LIO), while the other discards discrete filtering altogether and fits continuous-time splines directly to raw LiDAR and IMU residuals. However, the latter approach is computationally heavy, fragile under aggressive motions, and introduces substantial state update latency.

CT-SGAL-LIO takes a completely different path: "Leave the discrete LIO estimator and its map untouched, and simply clean up the emitted pose stream afterward." By holding recent poses in a small buffer and allowing a tiny fixed lag $\ell$, the trajectory can be queried via interpolation. Because it interpolates rather than extrapolates, it recovers very smooth and accurate poses and velocities while strictly adhering to online causality.

captions.F1: Conceptual view of CT-SGAL-LIO. Incoming discrete posterior poses are held in a fixed-lag buffer, and a robust cubic polynomial is fitted in the local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ tangent space. Evaluating the trajectory at $t_k^\star = t_k - \ell$, slightly behind the current time $t_k$, yields smoothed poses and velocities via stable interpolation instead of extrapolation.

sections.heading: The evolution of manifold LIO and continuous-time trajectory estimation
sections.summary: This section surveys recent developments in discrete manifold-based LIO alongside continuous-time approaches using splines. The proposed work sets itself apart by placing a fully decoupled continuous-time refinement layer on top of a state-of-the-art Galilean LIO system.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans three main categories:

### II-A Discrete-Time LIO on Manifolds
Starting from geometric feature-based methods like LOAM, the field progressed toward tightly coupled iterated Kalman filtering (IKFoM) that registers raw point clouds directly into incremental kd-trees (ikd-Tree), as in FAST-LIO and FAST-LIO2. State spaces have similarly grown from simple product manifolds $\mathrm{SO}(3) \times \mathbb{R}^6$ to $\mathrm{SE}_2(3)$ (which couples rotation and translation), and further to the Galilean group $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$ that incorporates the temporal coordinate. This paper builds on LIMOncello, a top-performing discrete LIO running on $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$. The proposed method leaves this estimator intact and simply ingests the projected $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ posterior pose sequence.

### II-B Continuous-Time Trajectory Estimation
To correct for intra-scan motion distortion, trajectory representations can be formulated as continuous functions of time. Examples include piecewise linear formulations like CT-ICP, as well as cubic B-spline models like CLIC, SLICT2, and RESPLE. However, because these systems optimize spline control points directly against raw sensor residuals, the estimator itself must be continuous-time, which brings high computational cost and vulnerability during aggressive dynamics. CT-SGAL-LIO differs fundamentally: it operates solely on the posterior poses emitted by a discrete estimator, remaining fully decoupled.

### II-C Smoothing and Fixed-Lag Estimation in LiDAR Odometry
Fixed-lag smoothing has long been used in factor graph backends and sliding-window optimization. Some systems, such as Wildcat, fit B-splines using iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), but they embed the spline inside the estimation loop to feed updates back into raw point correspondences. CT-SGAL-LIO performs no such feedback. Operating as a pure post-processing layer, it can be attached to any LIO that outputs a pose stream.

sections.heading: A plug-and-play post-processing pipeline for existing LIO
sections.summary: The system consists of two parts: a discrete $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$ estimator and the downstream CT-SGAL-LIO refinement layer. The estimator and its mapping pipeline remain completely unaffected, while the emitted posterior pose stream is smoothly reconstructed within a bounded memory window.
sections.details:
The overall architecture is clean and modular (see Fig. F2).

Upfront, a discrete $\mathrm{SGal}(3)$ LIO estimator (LIMOncello) runs continuously. It alternates forward IMU propagation with iterated error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) updates against LiDAR scan matches, streaming posterior states at high rates.

Downstream, CT-SGAL-LIO consumes this posterior state stream through three main steps:
- **Persistent Temporal Memory**: Newly arrived posterior poses and covariances are stored in a bounded temporal window, with stale states pruned automatically.
- **Robust Local Trajectory Fit**: Buffered poses are converted into tangent-space (Lie algebra) coordinates relative to a local anchor pose. A cubic polynomial is fitted using covariance weights, Huber loss, and a curvature regularization penalty to damp rapid oscillations.
- **Delayed State Evaluation**: The continuous trajectory is evaluated at a fixed-lag time $t_k^\star = t_k - \ell$, slightly in the past relative to $t_k$, producing smoothed poses, linear velocities, and angular velocities.

Because this layer is isolated from front-end point processing and map updates, it can be dropped into existing pipelines without breaking anything.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of CT-SGAL-LIO. Receiving posterior poses and covariances from the discrete SGal(3) LIO estimator on the left, the online trajectory layer on the right sequentially manages bounded memory, fits a local cubic polynomial, and evaluates the state at a fixed lag to output refined continuous-time states.

sections.heading: Robust cubic fitting via a fixed lag and local Lie algebra chart
sections.summary: Posterior poses are mapped to an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ Lie algebra chart relative to a local anchor, where a time-normalized cubic polynomial is solved via IRLS. By combining covariance weighting, Huber loss for outlier rejection, and curvature penalties to prevent oscillations, stable poses and velocities are derived analytically via fixed-lag interpolation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Problem Formulation
The input is a stream of timestamped poses $\mathbf{T}_i = (\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{p}_i) \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ and their covariance matrices $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$. The active time window in the buffer is $[t_k^\star - W, t_k]$, where $W$ is the past history length before the query timestamp and $\ell$ is the output latency (lag), placing the query at $t_k^\star = t_k - \ell$. Because $W > 0$ and $\ell > 0$, the query time sits safely inside the observed window. Rather than waiting for future data, looking back slightly via "fixed-lag interpolation" yields well-conditioned interpolation while maintaining causal, online execution.

To ensure numerical stability, time is normalized to $[-1, 1]$ using window center $c_k$ and half-width $h = (W + \ell)/2$, giving $u_i = (t_i - c_k)/h$. Direct polynomial fitting on rotation matrices violates $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ constraints. Instead, the first pose in the window $\mathbf{T}_{r,k}$ serves as a local reference, defining a 6D coordinate $\mathbf{z}_i$ from the translation offset $\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_{r,k}$ and the Lie algebra rotation vector $\mathrm{Log}(\mathbf{R}_{r,k}^\top \mathbf{R}_i)$. This vector is modeled using a cubic basis $\mathbf{b}(u) = [1, u, u^2, u^3]^\top$ and coefficient matrix $\mathbf{A}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 4}$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{z}}(u) = \mathbf{A}_k \mathbf{b}(u)$$
Pyr poses are mapped back via the matrix exponential $\mathrm{Exp}$, guaranteeing they remain strictly on $\mathrm{SO}(3)$.

The objective combines a Huber loss on covariance-weighted residuals with a second-derivative (curvature) penalty that suppresses spurious wiggles:
$$\min_{\mathbf{A}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_k} \rho_\delta (\|\mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}(u_i)\|_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i}^2) + \sum_{u_q \in \mathcal{Q}} \|\mathbf{A}\ddot{\mathbf{b}}(u_q)\|_{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^2$$

### IV-B Online Estimation and Implementation Details
This optimization is solved via Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS). Precision matrices $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i$ are built by clamping the eigenvalues of the input covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$, and Huber weights $w_i$ are updated based on residual magnitudes. Stacking the matrix coefficients into a 24D vector $\mathbf{a}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{24}$ reduces the normal equations to a compact $24 \times 24$ linear system, which can be solved extremely quickly regardless of trajectory length.

Once solved, the polynomial is evaluated at the fixed-lag point $u_k^\star$. Linear velocity $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_k^\star$ follows analytically from the time derivative of the cubic basis, while angular velocity $\hat{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k^\star$ is computed consistently via central differencing on the Lie group.

sections.heading: Real-world validation: cutting local jitter while protecting global accuracy
sections.summary: Evaluations across three public benchmarks (17 sequences) and a 19.5-minute dataset show that CT-SGAL-LIO reduces short-horizon relative trajectory error (RTE) by up to 70% and suppresses pose jumps by 85.4% over long runs, without degrading absolute trajectory error (ATE).
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
The method was evaluated on 17 sequences across GRAND-TOUR (4 sequences, Hesai XT32 + NovAtel CPT7), MCD NTU Campus (6 sequences, Livox Mid-70 + VectorNav VN100), and GEODE (7 sequences, Velodyne VLP-16 + Xsens MTi-30). Baselines included the discrete LIMOncello estimator, RESPLE (which embeds continuous splines in a Kalman filter), and FAST-LIO2. Metrics were Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE RMSE) for global accuracy and Relative Trajectory Error (RTE RMSE) over a short interval ($\Delta t = 0.1$ s) for local smoothness.

### V-B Qualitative Evaluation
On the MCD day01 sequence (Fig. F3), the estimated trajectory and temporal ATE profile overlap almost perfectly with LIMOncello. When looking at RTE plotted across various time horizons, however, CT-SGAL-LIO achieves substantially lower errors at short intervals, confirming that high-frequency local oscillations are removed without accumulating global drift.

In the 19.5-minute R-Campus experiment (Fig. F4, ~120,000 states), the 95th-percentile inter-state position velocity dropped from $16.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ down to $2.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$—an $85.4\%$ reduction. Even so, the 3D end-to-start closure gap shifted by merely $4.7\,\mathrm{mm}$ upon returning to the start point. This demonstrates long-term stability without warping global geometry.

### V-C Quantitative Results
- **GRAND-TOUR**: CT-SGAL-LIO achieved the lowest RTE on all 4 sequences, cutting RTE by roughly 67% over LIMOncello on HAUS_1, with matching or better ATE.
- **MCD**: Ranked 1st or 2nd in RTE across all 6 day/night runs, remaining stable across extreme lighting changes without sacrificing global accuracy.
- **GEODE**: Across 7 challenging sequences with stairs and rough ground, RTE was reduced by 9.9% to 51.1% over LIMOncello. On Offroad1–3, it achieved the best ATE and RTE among all tested methods.

### V-D Ablation Studies
Component ablations on the GEODE dataset confirmed several design choices:
- **Fixed Lag**: Adding a lag of $\ell = 0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ for interpolation improved RTE by another $7.9\%$ compared to an extrapolation model evaluated at zero lag.
- **Curvature Term**: Removing the curvature penalty nearly doubled the 99th-percentile local residual, showing it is vital for smoothness.
- **Huber Loss**: When synthetic translation spikes ($0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ impulses) were injected, the Huber loss contained the 99th-percentile residual to $0.482\,\mathrm{mm}$ versus $0.721\,\mathrm{mm}$ without it, demonstrating robustness to sudden outlier poses.

captions.F3: Comparison on MCD NTU Campus (day01). While (a) the estimated trajectory and (b) ATE over time closely match the baseline globally, (c) RTE plotted against evaluation interval $\Delta t$ reveals that CT-SGAL-LIO dramatically lowers error over short horizons.
captions.F4: Long-term behavior during a 19.5-minute R-Campus run. (a) Global trajectory consistency is preserved across 120,000 states, with an end-to-start gap change of only 4.7 mm. (b) The 95th percentile of inter-state velocity spikes drops by 85.4%, from 16.5 m/s to 2.4 m/s.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: CT-SGAL-LIO is a lightweight, causal module that refines discrete LIO outputs via fixed-lag continuous-time cubic fitting. It drastically suppresses local oscillations while preserving global accuracy. Future work includes extending it to other LIO backends and adapting window sizes to vehicle motion.
sections.details:
This work introduced CT-SGAL-LIO, a causal, fixed-lag continuous-time refinement layer designed to smooth posterior pose streams from discrete LiDAR-inertial odometry.

Its key advantage is modularity: it acts as a standalone post-processor without modifying the underlying filter or map representation. By coupling covariance-weighted cubic polynomial fitting on a local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ Lie algebra chart with fixed-lag interpolation, it damps short-horizon jitter while respecting online causal execution.

Across three benchmarks and an extensive real-world trial, the module reduced relative trajectory error (RTE) by up to 70% and suppressed state jumps by 85.4%, leaving global trajectory error (ATE) intact. In sequences where the discrete posterior already lacked noticeable jitter, however, the relative improvement was modest.

The authors plan to open-source the code and benchmark results to support community validation, with future plans to apply the framework to other discrete LIO frontends and explore motion-adaptive tuning for the lag and window lengths.

takeaways: Brings attention to a common yet overlooked practical issue: even globally accurate LIO outputs suffer from short-horizon jitter caused by alternating IMU propagation and LiDAR updates.

Instead of rebuilding the whole estimator around complex continuous-time models, treating discrete poses as pseudo-measurements and interpolating with a fixed-lag cubic polynomial offers a far better balance of compute, robustness, and accuracy.
Formulating the fit on a local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ chart caps the normal equations to a tiny $24 \times 24$ linear system, making real-time execution effortless regardless of trajectory duration.
Serves as an immediate drop-in upgrade for downstream tasks—like motion control and path tracking—that require high-rate, smooth pose and velocity estimates.
limitations: Introducing a fixed lag (set to $\ell = 0.2$ s in the paper) creates inherent output latency, presenting a tradeoff for downstream feedback controllers requiring ultra-low latency.
On sequences where the baseline discrete LIO exhibits little to no pose jitter, the resulting RTE reduction is minor (often under 10%).
Hyperparameters like window length $W$, lag $\ell$, and curvature weight $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ are currently static, lacking dynamic adaptation to aggressive maneuvers or stationary conditions.
